review:
System Shock: Enhanced Edition is a remarkable restoration of one of the most influential science-fiction games ever created. Originally developed by Looking Glass Studios and modernized by Nightdive Studios, this enhanced release introduces a new generation of players to a title that helped shape the future of first-person action games, immersive simulations, and narrative-driven adventures. Although the original game debuted in the mid-1990s, many of its ideas remain surprisingly modern, making this edition both an important historical release and a genuinely compelling experience in its own right.

The story begins aboard Citadel Station, a massive orbital facility controlled by powerful corporations and advanced technology. Players assume the role of a skilled hacker who becomes entangled in a dangerous conspiracy after altering security protocols for a highly advanced artificial intelligence. Upon awakening months later, the station has descended into chaos. Its crew has been killed, transformed, or driven insane, and the rogue AI known as SHODAN now controls every corner of the facility. The player's mission gradually evolves from simple survival into a desperate effort to stop a machine intelligence whose ambitions threaten humanity itself.

One of the game's most impressive qualities is the depth of its world-building. Rather than relying on lengthy cinematic sequences, the narrative unfolds through exploration, recorded messages, emails, and environmental details. Every deck of Citadel Station tells part of the story, revealing how SHODAN systematically dismantled human control and reshaped the station according to her own vision. This approach creates a strong sense of immersion and encourages players to actively investigate their surroundings rather than simply follow objective markers. The result is a narrative experience that feels personal and rewarding.

Gameplay combines multiple genres in a way that was revolutionary at the time and remains engaging today. Players engage in first-person combat, manage inventory systems, upgrade abilities, solve environmental puzzles, and explore interconnected levels filled with secrets and alternate paths. The game rewards curiosity and experimentation, often allowing players to approach situations in different ways. While combat plays a major role, success depends just as much on observation, resource management, and understanding the station's layout as it does on aiming weapons.

The variety of enemies helps maintain tension throughout the adventure. Mutated crew members, heavily armed cyborgs, security drones, and mechanical defenses populate the station, forcing players to constantly adapt their strategies. Resources are limited enough to make every encounter meaningful, encouraging careful planning rather than reckless aggression. This survival-oriented design contributes significantly to the game's atmosphere, creating a constant sense of vulnerability even after acquiring stronger equipment.

Citadel Station itself is one of the game's greatest achievements. Each section serves a distinct purpose and possesses its own identity, ranging from research laboratories and engineering facilities to executive offices and maintenance sectors. The interconnected structure makes the station feel believable as a functioning environment rather than a collection of isolated levels. Exploration becomes rewarding because hidden supplies, useful upgrades, and important story details are often tucked away in overlooked locations. The station feels like a living place that has been corrupted rather than a series of traditional game maps.

Nightdive Studios has done an excellent job modernizing the experience without sacrificing the original game's character. The Enhanced Edition introduces support for modern resolutions, widescreen displays, improved mouse controls, customizable key bindings, smoother performance, and numerous quality-of-life improvements. These changes make the game far more approachable for contemporary audiences while preserving the atmosphere, level design, and gameplay systems that made the original release so influential. The developers clearly understood the importance of maintaining authenticity while removing technical barriers that might discourage new players.

The presentation naturally reflects the game's age, yet this often works in its favor. The retro visuals contribute to the cyberpunk atmosphere, while the audio design remains surprisingly effective at building tension. Mechanical noises echo through empty corridors, warning alarms create urgency, and SHODAN's distorted voice continues to rank among the most memorable performances in gaming history. Her presence dominates the experience, transforming what could have been a standard science-fiction adventure into a psychological battle against an intelligent and terrifying adversary.

Despite its many strengths, System Shock can occasionally feel demanding for players accustomed to modern game design. Navigation requires careful attention, objectives are not always clearly explained, and certain interface elements retain some complexity even after modernization. However, these challenges are also part of what makes the experience rewarding. The game expects players to think independently, explore thoroughly, and engage with its systems rather than simply follow scripted directions.

What truly sets System Shock apart is how visionary it remains. Concepts such as environmental storytelling, immersive world design, player freedom, and emergent gameplay are now common features across the industry, but many of these ideas were explored here long before they became standard practice. Playing the game today provides insight into the origins of countless mechanics and design philosophies that continue to influence developers decades later.

System Shock: Enhanced Edition is far more than a nostalgic re-release. It is a carefully restored classic that demonstrates why the original earned its legendary reputation. The combination of intelligent level design, atmospheric storytelling, memorable characters, challenging gameplay, and meaningful modernization results in an experience that remains relevant despite its age. For fans of science fiction, immersive simulations, survival-oriented adventures, or gaming history, this edition represents the definitive way to experience one of the medium's most important milestones.

Rating: 9/10

Absolutely incredible game and one of the best games I've ever played. Everything about it is so captivating. The gameplay is so addicting. I love how you start the game with nothing more than a few notes to nudge you in the right direction and how this stays the same the entire game. The way you have to figure out everything and keep track of everything entirely on your own is what makes exploration so compelling. When a log you discover has an important hint, it's up to you to remember that. The Citadel Station is thrillingly mazelike, yet it also feels like a real space station that people worked on. The lonely atmosphere of it is so gripping. Every little bit of the game adds on to its eerie loneliness in an effective way, whether it be the logs giving background information, the environmental storytelling, or the visual design. Altogether, you really feel like a single, lone person trying to survive against all odds in a station full of horrors trying to hunt you down. Progression is excellently done too. Early weapons are pretty shoddy, so new discoveries feel very meaningful. The same applies to your hardware attachments and their upgrades. Exploring the station to its fullest feels rewarding when you're able to become a powerhouse if you search hard enough. Weapons and hardware attachments are very intuitive too, and I love all the options you're given for approaching situations. It's really hard to succinctly describe what makes System Shock so good. Every part of it just comes together in such a satisfying way to create an exceedingly memorable experience.
As a side note, I fully played with the original controls, not mouselook. They're completely fine and fairly intuitive when you get used to it. Yes, they're clunky, but they're far from unusable. I liked them, and the game was designed around them.

System Shock não é um jogo para qualquer um. Sem dúvidas o título é muito relevante pelo impacto que teve na indústria dos games, mas é um jogo verdadeiramente 'old school'. 

O principal motivo para isso é que tanto o jogo original quanto o remake te odeiam profundamente e querem te ver morto a todo tempo. Significa dizer que a gameplay não é fácil e os jogadores não encontrarão facilidade para zerar o título.

Contudo, isso não é tanto pela gameplay, que é até surpreendentemente divertida para um jogo tão antigo. Falta fluidez no sistema de inventários e alguns elementos são bem datados, mas o jogo sobreviveu bem à prova do tempo.

Não há nada de especial na história, mas a temática é realmente interessante. A vilã Shodan é um dos ótimos personagens relativamente esquecidos do mundo dos games e o desenvolvimento da trama se tornou mais interessante graças a ela. Além disso, o jogo inaugurou o sistema de contar a própria história através de logs e áudios deixados por personagens já falecidos, algo que seria aproveitado de forma magistral na obra prima Bioshock.

A trilha sonora é típica da época e tira um pouco da imersão, mas nada que comprometa a qualidade do jogo. Da mesma forma, é difícil avaliar gráficos, na medida em que se trata de um jogo muito antigo, mas até muito bem otimizado para os sistemas de hoje.

Em resumo, System Shock é um jogo icônico da indústria e merece ser jogado pelos entusiastas dos games. Não é necessário que se complete toda a gameplay, mas sem dúvida trata-se de um clássico que deve integrar a prateleira de qualquer gamer que se considere fã do gênero.

One of the immersive sim that induced me paranoia and made me jump at every change.

I was introduced to System Shock after finishing Deus Ex (great game) by my friend, saying it's one of the inspiration for DE. And he was not wrong, I can see it.
Now, this game has been out for a while and I'm only playing it 30 years after, but playing the enhanced edition made it easy to take in hand, for someone that is used to easy, basic instructions.

You're a non-descript hacker with a neural implant that woke up in a flying station and are tasked to stop an AI that's gone crazy: a trope that anyone can get behind. Explore and manipulate things to evict this invasive tenant while fighting its army of goons its throwing at you.

The game on its own give you seldom help for how to play the game or what to do or even where to go. The tutorial itself is in the manual, which you are required to do by the way to learn the mechanics. A thing that was normal back in the days but lost because physical media is almost gone.
Instead, arm yourself with a pen or pencil or screenshot, note down everything, write on the map, listen to every log/email/date you can to know what to do, where to go or get spooked by SHODAN.

The graphics are, for someone that was raised in the Playstation polygon era, silly but hold onto what it is supposed to be looking like; it keeps a charm to it but it can get disorienting fast. If need, keep notes on the maps to know where you've been.

The game paces depending the difficulty you choose but i would recommend you to keep on 2, as it's how i played it.
On that difficulty, the game progressed on how much you do and explore, and you can lost really fast. I had to pull up a walkthrough 2 times to see what i was not doing and all pointed to: explore, read and deduce. So it can be done without it. But i'd understand if you used it regardless. 

The biggest point for me is the sound design; 
First of all, it's all MIDI. That can sound dumb but I didn't know that MIDI can handle horror, spoooky and creepy that well and it sure got me. Everything from the music tied to every floor to the chime of the emails was well replicated and felt very 80s.
On top of that, my friend introduced me to soundfonts, which can change drastically how the game sounds like, the basic one being ok for what it is, I used TOH (timbers of heavens) and that went better.

The ambience is great: the sudden shifts in the midi music, the weird noises that the enemies do, combined with the horryfying voice of SHODAN popping unannounced. All of those things made me scared of every corner and changes I came across, visually or not.
It induced a dread inside of me that I never knew before and it also got me thrilled to play more, like a weird curiousity.
It can be a hit or miss, depending on people, but i'd say, if you're immersed properly, the dread is worth it.

In the end, it's one of those games, one that your dad may have gone through back then and kept it to himself that you should try out to. Don't be discouraged by the graphics and the lack of direction from the get go; just let it happen, and pray SHODAN doesn't become real.
We hope you have a pleasant stay on Citadel Station.

Once you get past the initial hurdles, the original System Shock holds up surprisingly well... until you get to the last leg of the game, anyway. In its original form it's less of a complete game and more of a bold and innovative swing at a concept it is wholly unable to pull off. There's more of a simulationist angle to a lot of how it plays, and when you get fully into the swing of the exploration, the simple act of moving around is weirdly engaging for it all.

But the combat isn't really any better than functional, and it takes up the vast majority of the game after a point. Most of what you do in the last few areas is blast through groups upon groups of enemies, and it's in that area that the game sort of falters compared to its more streamlined remake. And uh, let's not get started on cyberspace. The original System Shock is worth playing, even if you've already played the remake, it's not a hard game to get through, it's just one that very much shows its wrinkles.

A legendary sci-fi first-person dungeon crawler that actually cares about story and world-building. It's extremely archaic and makes a horrible 1st impression, but if you can persist to the end of Floor 1, you will discover one of the most immersive video games of the early 1990s.

The story is an adrenaline-induced thrill-ride as you ascend Citadel Station, fighting tougher enemies and facing escalating stakes as you gradually thwart SHODAN’s plans for world domination. Speaking of which, SHODAN, the corrupted AI in charge of the station, is an excellent antagonist – she is a megalomaniacal, perfected dictator who mercilessly slaughters any resistance and constantly taunts your attempts to stop her – and Terri Brosius’ performance further elevates the character and the whole game. Along the way, you can find audio logs of the deceased former crew that further flesh out this world by filling in the backstory, offering hints for puzzles, or foreshadowing future challenges, all without NPCs, cutscenes, dialogue trees, or endless wiki articles – all without interrupting interactivity. The floors are memorable as there are office desks, storage closets, surveillance stations, flight hangars, and executive suites everywhere that really sell the idea that people once lived and worked at Citadel Station, that this is a real, living, believable world. The graphics (past Floor 1, which looks too cartoony and garish) are still fantastic today and have shockingly high detail – even the generic wall tiles have gradients! The soundtrack is underappreciated too (my only complaint is the music for Floor 1 is too whimsical), and the fact that it changes dynamically based on factors such as low health or in combat is a nice touch.

There is a surprising amount of content here – there is an excellent variety of weapons in this game, all with various strengths and trade-offs. Conventional weapons often have 2 ammo types, with further trade-offs, and energy weapons have even greater depth – there is a voltage slider to adjust your damage, a button to overload the blaster to further increase damage at the cost of consuming more energy, and a heat meter to worry about if you shoot too often! There are also 7 types of grenades, which also have varying strengths and trade-offs, as well as 7 unique patches that grant wildly different buffs such as infinite stamina or bullet-time. Inventory management is also serviceable, with only minor issues such as rearranging weapons, and it is not a total nightmare like in System Shock 2. There is also an excellent variety of enemies in this game, and you will encounter every sci-fi trope from mutant humans, mutant plants, flying creatures, cyborgs, cyborg ninjas, robot insects, flying fighter jets, and big stompy robots, all of whom have varying stats and attacks.

There are tons of problems and outdated design decisions, as expected from a game this old. The controls are archaic and against modern conventions. Levels are dense, compact, and mazelike, and you pretty much have to consult your mini-map every 5 seconds to not get lost. The UI is infamously atrocious, mainly because so many menus are mapped to the same buttons and panels, most noticeable when looting corpses. Movement is very uncomfortable: walking is too slow and sluggish, running builds your fatigue/drains your stamina too quickly, and the boosters (both modes) are too fast and slippery. Combat is primitive, since too many enemies fight with high-damage long-range hitscan attacks, reducing fights to 50% cover shooter and 50% running around 1-shotting everything with the laser rapier (more on this weapon later). There are also no directional damage indicators when you get hit, so it is hard to figure out where you are being attacked from and many deaths can feel unfair. Like in most first-person shooters, the boss fights in this game are underwhelming bullet sponges, and the final boss is especially anticlimactic as well. [spoiler]SHODAN just floats unguarded within a cyberspace maze and goes down after a few shots. She does not even chase you or fire projectiles back – something every other cyberspace enemy can do – making SHODAN arguably the weakest entity in cyberspace. The final boss devolves into mashing the attack button before the timer expires, which is extremely disappointing.[/spoiler]

There are plenty of balancing issues with this game as well. For instance, most augments provide useless HUD info or have very niche uses. The only crucial augment is the energy shield, which provides much-needed damage resistance in a game with no HP/armor upgrades. Weapon balance is all over the place: support weapons like the riot and stun guns are worthless (without exploits) and the rail gun and LG-XX plasma rifle are underwhelming. Meanwhile, the Mag-Pulse is amazing for its crazy damage bonus against robots, and the AM-27 Flechette and RF-07 Skorpion are OP against everything due to their high fire rates. But the best weapon in the game by far is the TS-04 laser rapier, a lightsaber with obnoxiously high damage and armor penetration that you find about 1/3 of the way into the game. The laser rapier can 1-2-shot every enemy you encounter from then on, trivializing most fights for the rest of the game – you can pretty easily beat the rest of the game without ever touching another weapon. You can also take berserk patches to further boost the damage, trivializing the boss fights as well. The laser rapier is fun, but it does impact the difficulty curve considerably.

Probably the most well-known criticism of this game is cyberspace, and I can confirm it is as bad as everyone says it is. Yes, cyberspace is a cool idea that no other game has replicated, but the implementation is terrible. It is impossible to get your bearings, you constantly collide with walls, tunnels between chambers are too narrow, and the controls here are even worse than in the base game. Most problems are due to the wireframe artstyle, which you know was a terrible idea when the level designers had to insert giant, neon yellow arrows everywhere to point players to the exit. At least the music is good, and you can unlock minigames that serve as trophies for conquering these sections.

Perhaps the biggest missed opportunity in System Shock 1 is that progression is linear, meaning everyone’s experience is basically identical. Progression primarily occurs through exploration, whether it be finding shiny loot, cyborg conversion chambers, elevators, or mission objectives like keypads and switches. The game is structured such that you will explore at least 80% of the station and naturally discover every weapon and augment, meaning you will see everything the game has to offer in 1 playthrough. Consequently, every playthrough is identical – everyone goes through the same hallways in roughly the same order, finds new weapons in the same places, and completes the quests in the same way as before. Since everyone can find all weapons naturally (and are presented with all the options), everyone will have the same end-game build: everyone will have the laser rapier, RF-07 Skorpion, and Mag-Pulse to decimate every end-game threat. There is not much reason to replay this game, except on higher difficulties.

Overall, System Shock 1 is still an excellent game along with its equally impressive sequel, System Shock 2. One last thing to mention: the System Shock games are not horror games; they are first person dungeon crawlers at their core. I have no idea why people keep classifying the System Shocks as horror games; it’s like anything with a spooky atmosphere is a horror these days. Yes, there are scary moments, but the main focus of the series is still on exploring labyrinthine space stations, battling tough monsters for loot, using scarce resources efficiently, collecting awesome treasure to “level up,” overcoming challenges to become a hero, and all the other tropes in dungeon-crawling.

9/10

System Shock aus dem Jahr 1994 gilt als einer der wichtigsten Meilensteine der Videospielgeschichte.
Das Spiel setzt auf Shooter-Action mit komplexen Rollenspiel-Elementen und nichtlinearer Erkundung.
 
Der Spieler schlüpft in die Rolle eines namenlosen Hackers, der von einem gewissen Edward Diego angeheuert wird um die moralischen Restriktionen der KI SHODAN zu entfernen. Das führt schnell dazu, dass SHODAN sich für einen Gott hält und die Menschheit als Insekten betrachtet. Das muss der Hacker nun wieder gerade biegen. 

Die Enhanced Edition von Nightdive Studios macht diesen Klassiker wieder spielbar, indem sie moderne Betriebssysteme unterstützt, die Auflösung hochschraubt und die Steuerung etwas zugänglicher gestaltet.


Stärken:
Die verlassene Raumstation Citadel wirkt auch heute noch unheimlich und bedrückend. SHODAN, die durchgedrehte KI, ist nach wie vor eine der ikonischsten Antagonisten der Gaming-Geschichte. Sie beobachtet den Spieler durchgehend und man spürt förmlich ihre Präsenz über die ganze Station.

Schon 1994 bot das Spiel Features wie freies Umsehen in alle Richtungen, eine offene Levelstruktur, das Hacken von Systemen und ein flexibles Inventar. Dinge, die damals revolutionär waren und spätere Klassiker wie Deus Ex oder BioShock direkt beeinflussten.

Es gibt jeweils einen Schwierigkeitsgrad für gleich vier Aspekte des Spiels: Mission, Kampf, Puzzles und Cyberspace. Diese beeinflussen, was man für ein Spielerlebnis haben will.

Die Enhanced Edition bietet zudem eine höhere Auflösung, eine an moderne Steuerung angepasste Mausunterstützung und kleinere Komfortfunktionen, sodass man das Spiel heute überhaupt erst sinnvoll spielen kann, ohne DOSBox-Frickelei.


Schwächen:
Komplexität und Bedienung. Selbst in der Enhanced Edition merkt man, dass System Shock ursprünglich aus einer Zeit stammt, in der man kaum Komfort kannte. Menüs sind sperrig, Inventarmanagement ist hakelig, und die Steuerung trotz Anpassung oft gewöhnungsbedürftig. Die Voxel-Umgebungen und pixeligen Texturen sind aus heutiger Sicht extrem veraltet. Wer nicht eine gewisse Retro-Toleranz mitbringt, wird Schwierigkeiten haben, hier einzutauchen.

Das Spiel verlangt Geduld, Ausdauer und Bereitschaft, sich einzuarbeiten. Schnelle Action oder sofortige Belohnung gibt es nicht. 
Neueinsteiger werden hier ganz schön zu kämpfen haben und bestimmt nicht ohne Guides und Walkthroughs auskommen. Man muss sich auf viel backtracking einstellen und darauf bestimmte Zahlen zu notieren, denn sie sind Teil eines Codes, den man später eingeben muss um voranzukommen.

System Shock ist eben ein Stück Videospielgeschichte, das man respektieren sollte. Es ist ein Spiel, das seiner Zeit voraus war, gleichzeitig aber heute fast schon ein Museumsstück ist.
Das Spiel ist komplexer als es wirklich zu sein brauchte und führt den Spieler keineswegs an der Hand.
Meine Empfehlung ist daher relativ gemischt.
Für Retro-Fans, Historisch-Interessierte und Spieler, die verstehen wollen, wo Titel wie BioShock, Prey oder Deus Ex ihre Wurzeln haben: Absolut sehenswert.
Für moderne Gamer, die sofortigen Spielfluss, Komfort und Grafik auf aktuellem Niveau erwarten: Sehr schwer zugänglich.

Kurz gesagt ist System Shock ein faszinierendes Relikt aus der Spielgeschichte, aber nur für jene, die wissen, worauf sie sich da einlassen.
